title: Taiwan's local polls, a record-wet spring and robot dogs on the ward

stories.headline: Taiwan votes in 'nine-in-one' local elections seen as mid-term test
stories.headlineZh: 台湾举行“九合一”地方选举，被视为期中考验
stories.summaryZh: 台湾逾一万一千个地方职位同日改选，结果或影响2028年大选，也牵动澳大利亚能源出口。
stories.c1:
Millions of Taiwanese voters head to the polls on Saturday in what are known as the "nine-in-one" elections, so called because nine tiers of local office are contested at once, ranging from the mayors of the six major municipalities right down to village chiefs. More than 11,000 positions are up for grabs, and roughly 19.6 million people are eligible to cast a ballot at upwards of 18,000 polling stations, although, unlike in Australia, voting is not compulsory.

Held every four years, halfway through the presidential cycle, the polls are widely regarded as a mid-term report card for President Lai Ching-te and his Democratic Progressive Party (DPP). The stakes are considerable: in 2022 the opposition Kuomintang (KMT), which favours closer ties with Beijing, captured 14 of Taiwan's 22 cities and counties, a result seen as a serious blow to the DPP. Some analysts believe this year's outcome could shape the 2028 presidential race.

Yet the campaigns have revolved less around cross-strait tensions than around bread-and-butter concerns such as housing affordability, public transport and youth employment. The most closely watched contest is in Taipei, where the KMT's Chiang Wan-an, a great-grandson of Chiang Kai-shek, is seeking a second term against Puma Shen, a DPP lawmaker whom Beijing has sanctioned. Taiwan has warned of possible Chinese interference, which the head of its Mainland Affairs Council described as "inevitable", while Beijing dismisses such claims as fabricated.

For Australia, the result is not merely of academic interest. Taiwan is a critical link in global supply chains for AI and smart devices, and Australia supplies almost half of its coal and 38 per cent of its LNG. With a referendum on nuclear power held alongside the vote, any shift in Taiwan's energy policy could ripple through Australian exports.
stories.b2:
On Saturday, Taiwan is voting in the "nine-in-one" elections. The name means that nine levels of local government are chosen on the same day, from big-city mayors to village chiefs. More than 11,000 positions are available, and about 19.6 million people can vote. Voting is not compulsory.

These elections happen every four years, in the middle of the president's term. Many people see them as a test for President Lai Ching-te and his party, the DPP. In 2022, the opposition KMT, which wants closer ties with China, won 14 of the 22 cities and counties. Some experts think this year's result could affect the 2028 presidential election.

However, most candidates have focused on everyday problems such as housing costs, public transport and jobs for young people. The biggest race is in Taipei, where KMT mayor Chiang Wan-an wants a second term. His rival is Puma Shen, a DPP lawmaker sanctioned by China. Taiwan has warned that China may try to interfere, but Beijing says these claims are false.

The result also matters to Australia. Taiwan is an important part of global supply chains for AI and smart devices, and Australia sells it almost half of its coal and 38 per cent of its LNG. A vote on nuclear power could also change Taiwan's energy plans and affect Australian exports.

stories.headline: Storms cap off Australia's wettest El Niño spring on record
stories.headlineZh: 风暴为澳大利亚史上最湿润的厄尔尼诺春季收尾
stories.summaryZh: 厄尔尼诺通常带来干旱，但今年澳洲春季降雨创纪录；气象局预计夏季将异常炎热。
stories.c1:
Australia's soggy spring has gone out with a bang. A plume of humid tropical air swept across the east of the country this weekend, bringing widespread thunderstorms and raising the prospect of flash and river flooding in several states. It was a fitting finale to what has been the nation's wettest spring on record for an El Niño year.

Some of the downpours have been striking. Thargomindah, in outback Queensland, was drenched by 66 millimetres in under 12 hours, more than double its monthly average and its heaviest November rain in 35 years, while Warracknabeal in Victoria's Wimmera recorded more than 50 millimetres in a single hour. Minor flooding was possible across more than a dozen Victorian catchments, as well as parts of southern Queensland, NSW and even northern Tasmania, which had endured an exceptionally dry spell since August.

What makes the season remarkable is that El Niño is normally associated with drier conditions. Compared with 27 previous El Niño years since 1900, 2026 has set national records for the wettest El Niño year, winter-spring, October and spring. Pinning down the exact cause is difficult, but very warm Indian Ocean temperatures have fed extra moisture into the atmosphere, and an unusually strong high-pressure system near New Zealand may also have played a part.

Relief from the rain, however, may be short-lived, and not necessarily welcome. El Niño's influence on rainfall tends to fade by summer, and the Bureau of Meteorology expects a drier-than-normal season across much of tropical Australia. More worryingly, national temperatures are forecast to sit close to 2°C above the long-term average, potentially rivalling the record set in 2018–19.
stories.b2:
Australia's very wet spring ended with more storms this weekend. Warm, wet tropical air moved across the east of the country, bringing thunderstorms and the risk of flash flooding and river flooding in several states. It has been Australia's wettest spring on record for an El Niño year.

Some places received huge amounts of rain. Thargomindah in outback Queensland got 66 millimetres in less than 12 hours, which is more than twice its usual rain for the whole month. In Warracknabeal, in western Victoria, more than 50 millimetres fell in just one hour. Minor flooding was possible in many rivers in Victoria, southern Queensland, NSW and northern Tasmania.

This is unusual because El Niño usually brings drier weather to Australia. Compared with 27 earlier El Niño years since 1900, 2026 has broken national records for the wettest El Niño year, October and spring. It is hard to know the exact reason, but a very warm Indian Ocean has added extra moisture to the air.

The wet weather may not last. El Niño's effect on rain usually becomes weaker in summer, and the Bureau of Meteorology expects a drier summer than normal in much of tropical Australia. Summer is also likely to be very hot, with national temperatures forecast to be close to 2°C above the long-term average.

stories.headline: Sony's retired robot dogs find new homes in Japanese hospitals
stories.headlineZh: 索尼退役机器狗在日本医院找到新家
stories.summaryZh: 索尼回收修复旧款Aibo机器狗并送往医院，帮助病人缓解等待、鼓励孩子接受检查。
stories.c1:
In Japan, retired robot dogs are finding a second life in hospitals. Sony's Aibo, which first went on sale in 1999 and is no longer in production, is being donated by owners who can no longer keep their mechanical pets. Through an "adoption program" run by Tokyo-based Sony Group Corporation, the robots are repaired and upgraded before being rehomed in hospitals and other care facilities.

Packed with sensors and cameras, Aibo is programmed to remember its name, its owner's face and its surroundings. It barks, cocks its head, waddles towards people and appears to be delighted when petted. Yoshiyuki Katsuno, the Sony official who oversees the scheme, says owners often feel as though they are sending off their own child, and he believes the robots can get people talking and lift the spirits of those who are worn out.

At a university on the outskirts of Tokyo, ear, nose and throat doctor Manabu Komori says Aibo helps to ease the long waits faced by patients and has coaxed reluctant children into being examined. Admittedly, the hospital also uses real dogs to comfort patients, and Komori stops short of claiming that robots are superior. Still, a machine does not need feeding and is far less likely to be temperamental.

The program reflects a broader cultural appetite for cuteness in Japan, where "kawaii" is seen less as a weakness than as a quality that fosters harmony and communication. Whether such robots offer genuine companionship or merely a convincing imitation remains an open question, but for patients facing a daunting hospital visit, the distinction may matter little.
stories.b2:
In Japan, old robot dogs are being given new homes in hospitals. Sony's Aibo first went on sale in 1999, but it is no longer made. Some owners who cannot keep their robot pets have given them to Sony, which repairs and upgrades them through an "adoption program". Then they go to hospitals and care facilities.

Aibo has sensors and cameras, and it can remember its name, its owner's face and its surroundings. It barks, moves its head and walks towards people, and it seems happy when someone pets it. Yoshiyuki Katsuno, who runs the program at Sony, says owners feel like they are saying goodbye to their own child. He believes Aibo helps people talk to each other and can cheer up tired people.

Manabu Komori, a doctor at a university near Tokyo, says Aibo makes long waits easier for patients. It has also helped nervous children agree to be examined. The hospital uses real dogs too, and Komori does not say robots are better. However, a robot dog does not need food.

Cuteness, or "kawaii", is important in Japanese culture, where it is seen as something that helps people get along. People may disagree about whether a robot can be a real friend, but for nervous patients in hospital, it may not matter very much.

stories.headline: Victoria votes as polls point to the end of Labor's 12-year rule
stories.headlineZh: 维州投票日到来，民调显示工党12年执政或将终结
stories.summaryZh: 维州约一半选民已提前投票，民调显示联盟党有望获胜，单一民族党和绿党也备受关注。
stories.c1:
Victorians are casting their final votes today in a state election that polls suggest will bring 12 years of Labor government to an end. By the time polling booths opened, roughly half of the state's 4.7 million eligible voters had already voted, either at early voting centres or by post.

Labor's slide has been dramatic. The party has cycled through three leaders in four years: Daniel Andrews stepped down in 2023, and his successor, Jacinta Allan, resigned in July amid corruption allegations surrounding the Big Build infrastructure program and a contentious change to the emergency services levy. Her replacement, Ben Carroll, has ordered a royal commission into the allegations, but he has struggled to shake off soaring state debt and the legacy of his predecessors.

On the other side, Liberal leader Jess Wilson has worked to rebuild a party that has had three leaders since 2022, and the Coalition surged in the polls on law and order. Even so, she spent the final days of the campaign on the back foot after late revelations of planned privatisations and kinder cuts. To form government, the Coalition needs to pick up more than a dozen extra seats, a task that a resurgent One Nation could complicate.

Indeed, One Nation is expected to attract more than 20 per cent of the primary vote, despite a string of candidate controversies. The Greens, led by Ellen Sandell, are hoping to hold inner-city seats such as Melbourne, Richmond and Brunswick, though Sandell concedes these contests are "always incredibly close". Whatever the outcome, the winning party may well take office with a historically low primary vote.
stories.b2:
Victorians are voting in a state election today, and polls suggest that 12 years of Labor government will come to an end. About half of the state's 4.7 million eligible voters had already voted early or by post before election day.

Labor has had a difficult few years, with three leaders in four years. Daniel Andrews left in 2023. Then Jacinta Allan resigned in July after corruption claims about the Big Build program and an unpopular change to the emergency services levy. The new premier, Ben Carroll, ordered a royal commission, but high state debt has made his job harder.

Liberal leader Jess Wilson has tried to rebuild her party, which has had three leaders since 2022. The Coalition became more popular because of worries about crime. However, near the end of the campaign, Wilson had to defend plans for privatisations and kinder cuts. The Coalition needs to win more than 12 new seats to govern, and One Nation could make this harder.

One Nation is expected to win more than 20 per cent of the primary vote, even though several of its candidates have caused controversy. The Greens, led by Ellen Sandell, hope to keep inner-city seats such as Melbourne, Richmond and Brunswick. Whoever wins may have a very low primary vote compared with past governments.

dialogue.title: A Rainy Flat Inspection
dialogue.setting: Two friends meet outside a flat in Footscray for an inspection on a stormy morning.
dialogue.settingZh: 一个暴风雨的早上，两个朋友在富茨克雷的一间公寓外碰头看房。

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: Sorry I'm late — the tram was crawling because of the rain. Have I missed much?
lines.zh: 抱歉来晚了——下雨电车开得像蜗牛一样。我错过什么了吗？

lines.name: Tom
lines.en: Not at all. The agent's running behind too, so we've got a few minutes.
lines.zh: 完全没有。中介也迟到了，我们还有几分钟。

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: Good. It looks decent from the outside, but I'm a bit wary of the photos online.
lines.zh: 那就好。从外面看还不错，但我对网上那些照片有点存疑。

lines.name: Tom
lines.en: Same. They always use a wide-angle lens to make the rooms look twice the size.
lines.zh: 我也是。他们总用广角镜头，让房间看起来大一倍。

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: Exactly. I'm checking the bathroom for mould straight away, given all this rain.
lines.zh: 没错。下了这么多雨，我要先去浴室看看有没有霉。

lines.name: Tom
lines.en: Smart. And let's run the taps to see what the water pressure's like.
lines.zh: 聪明。我们再开开水龙头，看看水压怎么样。

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: Did the listing say whether parking's included? That could be a deal-breaker for me.
lines.zh: 房源信息有说包不包车位吗？这对我来说可能是决定性的。

lines.name: Tom
lines.en: It was a bit vague, so I'll bring it up with the agent.
lines.zh: 写得有点含糊，我会跟中介提一下。

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: Also, it's a bit of a hike to the station. Did you time the walk?
lines.zh: 还有，走到车站有点远。你计时过吗？

lines.name: Tom
lines.en: About twelve minutes. Not ideal, but it's doable if the rent's reasonable.
lines.zh: 大概十二分钟。不算理想，但如果房租合理还是可以接受的。

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: Fair enough. If it ticks most of the boxes, should we apply today?
lines.zh: 有道理。如果大部分条件都满足，我们今天就申请吗？

lines.name: Tom
lines.en: I reckon so. Places like this get snapped up within a day or two.
lines.zh: 我觉得行。这样的房子一两天内就会被抢光。

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: Right, here comes the agent. Let's play it cool and not look too keen.
lines.zh: 好，中介来了。我们装得淡定点，别显得太想要。
